questions.question: Name and explain at least 4 common causes of memory leaks in JavaScript.
questions.answer:
1. Forgotten event listeners: Listeners added to DOM nodes or global objects (window, document) that are never removed. Each listener is a closure that may capture large objects.

2. Detached DOM nodes: A node removed from the DOM but still referenced by a JS variable or closure — can't be GC'd.

3. Closures holding large scope: A closure unintentionally captures a huge array/object in its scope even if it only uses a tiny part of it.

4. Global variable accumulation: Variables accidentally created on window (missing var/let/const in sloppy mode) that grow unbounded.

5. SetInterval never cleared: A setInterval callback that captures objects and is never cleared — runs forever, holding references.

6. Circular references: Object A references B, B references A — old IE had issues with this; modern GC (mark-and-sweep) handles it.
questions.tip: Name the Chrome DevTools Memory panel and Heap Snapshot tool — it signals you've actually debugged this in production.

What is the difference between mark-and-sweep and reference counting GC?

questions.question: How does the mark-and-sweep garbage collection algorithm work? Why does it handle circular references but reference counting doesn't?
questions.answer:
Reference counting: Each object tracks how many references point to it. When count = 0, it's freed. Problem: if A references B and B references A, both have count ≥ 1 forever — they're never freed even if unreachable from the rest of the program.

Mark-and-sweep: The GC starts from a set of "roots" (global object, call stack). It marks every object reachable from roots. In the sweep phase, anything not marked is freed. Circular references are handled correctly because A↔B, if both are unreachable from any root, neither gets marked and both get swept.
questions.tip: Modern V8 uses a generational GC (minor/major heap), incremental marking, and concurrent sweeping — mentioning this shows you understand production JS runtimes.

questions.title: Closure holding large reference
questions.explanation:
Output: 0
fn closes over id (= 0) and also inadvertently keeps bigArr alive in memory because the closure's scope includes everything in setup(). In modern engines V8 may optimise this, but logically bigArr cannot be GC'd while fn exists. Best practice: extract only what you need into a small variable and nullify the large one.
questions.concept: Unintended large variable captured in closure

questions.title: Event listener memory leak pattern
questions.explanation:
Answer: 2 closures
Each call to attachHandler() creates a new closure over its own data object AND registers a new event listener. Neither is removed. After two calls, two handlers live on the document — each holding a reference to its own data, preventing GC. The fix: return a cleanup function and call removeEventListener.
questions.concept: Accumulating event listeners — each creates a closure

questions.title: Detached DOM + closure = leak
questions.explanation:
Answer: No — el is NOT garbage collected.
ref is a closure that captures el. Even though node = null removes the only external reference to the DOM element, ref still holds el in its closure scope. el stays in memory as long as ref exists. This is the classic detached DOM node memory leak.
questions.concept: Detached DOM node kept alive by closure
